as_extracts.description: They record, represent and compare data they have collected.

content_descriptions.name: VC2M3ST02 - Mathematics
content_descriptions.text: create and compare different graphical representations of data sets, including using software where appropriate; interpret the data in terms of the context

elaborations.name: VC2M3ST02-E01 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: comparing various student-generated data representations and describing their similarities and differences

elaborations.name: VC2M3ST02-E02 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: using digital tools and graphing software to construct graphs of data acquired through experiments or observation and interpreting the data and making inferences; for example, graphing data from a science experiment and interpreting the results

elaborations.name: VC2M3ST02-E03 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: selecting appropriate formats or layout styles to present data as information, depending on the type of data and the audience; for example, lists, tables, graphs and infographics

elaborations.name: VC2M3ST02-E04 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: using newspapers or magazines to find examples of different displays of data, interpreting and describing the information they present

as_extracts.name: MAT3-E17
as_extracts.description: Students use practical activities, observation or experiment to identify and describe outcomes and the likelihood of everyday events explaining reasoning.

content_descriptions.name: VC2M3P01 - Mathematics
content_descriptions.text: identify practical activities and everyday events that involve chance, and describe possible outcomes and events as ‘likely’ or ‘unlikely’ and identify some events as ‘certain’ or ‘impossible’, explaining reasoning

elaborations.name: VC2M3P01-E01 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: predicting what could happen next in practical activities that involve an element of chance, considering possible outcomes and using terms such as ‘likely’ or ‘unlikely’ to explain their predictions

elaborations.name: VC2M3P01-E02 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: classifying a list of everyday events or sorting a set of event cards according to how likely they are to happen, using the language of chance and giving reasons for classifications; and discussing how impossible outcomes cannot ever happen, and uncertain outcomes are affected by chance as they may or may not happen, whereas certain events must always happen so they are not affected by chance

elaborations.name: VC2M3P01-E03 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: making predictions and testing what would happen, for example, if 10 names were put in a box and names were then drawn out one at a time and replaced after each selection, discussing how likely it would be after 10 selections that all 10 names were drawn from the box or that one name was drawn multiple times

as_extracts.name: MAT3-E18
as_extracts.description: Students conduct repeated chance experiments and discuss variation in results.

content_descriptions.name: VC2M3P02 - Mathematics
content_descriptions.text: conduct repeated chance experiments; identify and describe possible outcomes, record the results, and recognise and discuss the variation

elaborations.name: VC2M3P02-E01 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: identifying the possible outcomes of a chance experiment, creating a tally chart to record results, carrying out a few trials and tallying the results for each trial, and then responding to the questions ‘How did your results vary for each trial?’ and ‘How do the results vary across the class?’

elaborations.name: VC2M3P02-E02 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: conducting repeated trials of chance experiments such as tossing a coin, throwing a dice, drawing a coloured or numbered ball from a bag, or using a coloured spinner with equal partitions, and identifying the variation in the number of heads/fives/reds between trials

strand_content_descriptions.name: VC2M3N01 - Mathematics
strand_content_descriptions.text: identify, explain and use the properties of odd and even numbers

elaborations.name: VC2M3N01-E01 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: identifying even numbers using skip counting by twos or by grouping even collections of objects in twos

elaborations.name: VC2M3N01-E02 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: explaining why all numbers that end in the digits 0, 2, 4, 6 and 8 are even and that numbers ending in 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9 are odd

elaborations.name: VC2M3N01-E03 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: explaining why some materials can be shared evenly between 2 people without leaving a remainder and some cannot

elaborations.name: VC2M3N01-E04 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: explaining the patterns involved in adding, subtracting and multiplying odd and even numbers (for example, even + even = even, odd + even = odd, odd + odd = even) and using this to decide whether answers to addition, subtraction and multiplication calculations are correct or not

elaborations.name: VC2M3N01-E05 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: following an algorithm consisting of a flow chart with a series of instructions and decisions to determine whether a number is even or odd; and using the algorithm to identify which elements of a set of numbers are divisible by 2

strand_content_descriptions.name: VC2M3N02 - Mathematics
strand_content_descriptions.text: recognise, represent and order natural numbers using naming and writing conventions for numerals beyond 10 000

elaborations.name: VC2M3N02-E01 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: moving materials from one place to another on a place value model to show renaming of numbers (for example, 1574 can be shown as one thousand, 5 hundreds, 7 tens and 4 ones, or as 15 hundreds, 7 tens and 4 ones)

elaborations.name: VC2M3N02-E02 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: using the repeating pattern of place value names and spaces within sets of 3 digits to name and write larger numbers: ones, tens, hundreds, ones of thousands, tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands, ones of millions, tens of millions; for example, writing four hundred and twenty-five thousand as 425 000

elaborations.name: VC2M3N02-E03 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: predicting and naming the number that is one more than 99, 109, 199, 1009, 1099, 1999, 10 009 … 99 999 and discussing what will change when one, one ten and one hundred is added to each

elaborations.name: VC2M3N02-E04 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: comparing the Hindu-Arabic numeral system to other numeral systems; for example, investigating the Japanese numeral system, 一、十、百、千、万

organising_ideas.name: Asia and Australia’s Engagement with Asia - VC2CCPASK1
organising_ideas.text: Peoples of the Asia region are diverse in their backgrounds, experiences, traditions, cultures, histories, stories, religions, beliefs, perspectives and languages.
organising_ideas.ccp: Asia and Australia’s Engagement with Asia

organising_ideas.name: Asia and Australia’s Engagement with Asia - VC2CCPASU1
organising_ideas.text: The nations of Asia influence historical and contemporary global relationships, including international responses to global developments and events.
organising_ideas.ccp: Asia and Australia’s Engagement with Asia

organising_ideas.name: Asia and Australia’s Engagement with Asia - VC2CCPASU2
organising_ideas.text: The peoples of Asia shape human endeavour through the arts and political, sporting, economic, technological and scientific domains.
organising_ideas.ccp: Asia and Australia’s Engagement with Asia

elaborations.name: VC2M3N02-E05 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: comparing, reading and writing the numbers involved in more than 60 000 years of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ presence on the Australian continent through timescales relating to pre-colonisation and post-colonisation

organising_ideas.name: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Histories and Cultures - VC2CCPACP1
organising_ideas.text: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities of Australia maintain a deep connection to, and responsibility for, Country and Place and have holistic values and belief systems that are connected to the land, sea, sky and waterways.
organising_ideas.ccp: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Histories and Cultures

organising_ideas.name: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Histories and Cultures- VC2CCPACP2
organising_ideas.text: The occupation and colonisation of the land now known as Australia by the British, under the now overturned doctrine of terra nullius, were experienced by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples as an invasion that denied their occupancy of, and connection to, Country and Place.
organising_ideas.ccp: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Histories and Cultures

organising_ideas.name: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Histories and Cultures - VC2CCPACP3
organising_ideas.text: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples are the Traditional Owners of Country and Place, protected in Australian law by the Native Title Act 1993, which recognises pre-existing sovereignty, continuing systems of law and customs, and connection to Country and Place.
organising_ideas.ccp: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Histories and Cultures

organising_ideas.name: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Histories and Cultures - VC2CCPAC1
organising_ideas.text: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander societies are diverse and have distinct cultural expressions, such as language, customs and beliefs. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples have the right to maintain, control, protect and develop their cultural expressions, while also maintaining the right to control, protect and develop culture as Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property.
organising_ideas.ccp: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Histories and Cultures

organising_ideas.name: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Histories and Cultures - VC2CCPAC2
organising_ideas.text: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ ways of life reflect unique ways of being, knowing, thinking and doing.
organising_ideas.ccp: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Histories and Cultures

organising_ideas.name: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Histories and Cultures - VC2CCPAC3
organising_ideas.text: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people belong to the world’s oldest continuous cultures. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples demonstrate resilience in the maintenance, practice and revitalisation of culture despite the many historic and enduring impacts of colonisation, and they continue to celebrate and share the past, present and future manifestations of their cultures.
organising_ideas.ccp: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Histories and Cultures

organising_ideas.name: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Histories and Cultures - VC2CCPAP1
organising_ideas.text: Australia has 2 distinct First Nations Peoples; each encompasses a diversity of nations across Australia. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples have occupied the Australian continent and adjacent islands from time immemorial.
organising_ideas.ccp: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Histories and Cultures

organising_ideas.name: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Histories and Cultures - VC2CCPAP2
organising_ideas.text: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples have sophisticated political, economic and social organisation systems, which include but are not limited to family and kinship structures, laws, traditions, customs, land tenure systems and protocols for strong governance and authority.
organising_ideas.ccp: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Histories and Cultures

organising_ideas.name: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Histories and Cultures - VC2CCPAP3
organising_ideas.text: The significant and ongoing contributions of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples and their histories and cultures are acknowledged locally, nationally and globally.
organising_ideas.ccp: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Histories and Cultures

strand_content_descriptions.name: VC2M3N03 - Mathematics
strand_content_descriptions.text: recognise and represent unit fractions including $\frac{1}{2}$, $\frac{1}{3}$, $\frac{1}{4}$, $\frac{1}{5}$ and $\frac{1}{10}$ and their multiples in different ways; combine fractions with the same denominator to complete the whole

elaborations.name: VC2M3N03-E01 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: recognising that unit fractions represent equal parts of a whole; for example, one-third is one of 3 equal parts of a whole

elaborations.name: VC2M3N03-E02 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: representing unit fractions and their multiples in different ways; for example, using a Think Board to represent three-quarters using a diagram, concrete materials, a situation and fraction notation

elaborations.name: VC2M3N03-E03 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: cutting objects such as oranges, sandwiches or playdough into halves, quarters or fifths and reassembling them to demonstrate (for example, two-halves make a whole, four-quarters make a whole), counting the fractions as they go

elaborations.name: VC2M3N03-E04 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: sharing collections of objects, such as icy pole sticks or counters, between 3, 4 and 5 people and connecting division with fractions; for example, sharing equally between 3 people gives $\frac{1}{3}$ of the collection to each and sharing equally between 5 people gives $\frac{1}{5}$ of the collection to each

strand_content_descriptions.name: VC2M3N04 - Mathematics
strand_content_descriptions.text: add and subtract two- and three-digit numbers using place value to partition, rearrange and regroup numbers to assist in calculations without a calculator

elaborations.name: VC2M3N04-E01 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: using partitioning and part-part-whole models and the inverse relationship between addition and subtraction to solve addition or subtraction problems, making informal written ‘jottings’ to keep track of the numbers if necessary

elaborations.name: VC2M3N04-E02 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: using physical or virtual grouped materials or diagrams to make proportional models of numbers to assist in calculations, for example, to calculate 214 + 325, representing 214 as 2 groups of 100, one group of 10 and 4 ones and 325 as 3 groups of 100, 2 groups of 10 and 5 ones, resulting in 5 groups of 100, 3 groups of 10 and 9 ones, which is 539

elaborations.name: VC2M3N04-E03 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: choosing between standard and non-standard place value partitions to assist with calculations, for example, to solve 485 + 365, thinking of 365 as 350 + 15, then adding the parts, 485 + 15 = 500, 500 + 350 = 850

elaborations.name: VC2M3N04-E04 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: solving subtraction problems efficiently by adding or subtracting a constant amount to both numbers to create an easier calculation; for example, 534 − 395, adding 5 to both numbers to make 539 − 400 = 139

elaborations.name: VC2M3N04-E05 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: justifying choices about partitioning and regrouping numbers in terms of their usefulness for particular calculations when solving problems

elaborations.name: VC2M3N04-E06 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: applying knowledge of place value to assist in calculations when solving problems involving larger numbers; for example, calculating the total crowd numbers for an agricultural show that lasts a week

strand_content_descriptions.name: VC2M3N05 - Mathematics
strand_content_descriptions.text: multiply and divide one- and two-digit numbers, representing problems using number sentences, diagrams and arrays, and using a variety of calculation strategies

elaborations.name: VC2M3N05-E01 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: applying knowledge of numbers and the properties of operations using a variety of ways to represent multiplication or division number sentences; for example, using a Think Board to show different ways of visualising 8 × 4, such as an array, a diagram and a worded problem

elaborations.name: VC2M3N05-E02 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: using part-part-whole and comparative models to visually represent multiplicative relationships and choosing whether to use multiplication or division to solve problems

elaborations.name: VC2M3N05-E03 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: matching or creating a problem scenario or story that can be represented by a given number sentence involving multiplication and division; for example, using given number sentences to create worded problems for others to solve

elaborations.name: VC2M3N05-E04 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: formulating connected multiplication and division expressions by representing situations from Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ cultural stories and dances about how they care for Country/Place, such as turtle egg gathering, using number sentences

organising_ideas.name: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Histories and Cultures - VC2CCPACP1
organising_ideas.text: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities of Australia maintain a deep connection to, and responsibility for, Country and Place and have holistic values and belief systems that are connected to the land, sea, sky and waterways.
organising_ideas.ccp: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Histories and Cultures

organising_ideas.name: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Histories and Cultures - VC2CCPAC2
organising_ideas.text: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ ways of life reflect unique ways of being, knowing, thinking and doing.
organising_ideas.ccp: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Histories and Cultures

organising_ideas.name: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Histories and Cultures - VC2CCPAP1
organising_ideas.text: Australia has 2 distinct First Nations Peoples; each encompasses a diversity of nations across Australia. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples have occupied the Australian continent and adjacent islands from time immemorial.
organising_ideas.ccp: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Histories and Cultures

strand_content_descriptions.name: VC2M3N06 - Mathematics
strand_content_descriptions.text: estimate the quantity of objects in collections and make estimates when solving problems to determine the reasonableness of calculations

elaborations.name: VC2M3N06-E01 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: estimating how much space a grid paper representation of a large number such as 20 200 will take up on the wall and how much paper will be required

elaborations.name: VC2M3N06-E02 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: estimating the number of people in a large gathering (for example, a school assembly) using known numbers (such as how many students per class)

elaborations.name: VC2M3N06-E03 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: choosing which place value they would estimate to for different situations; for example, choosing to estimate to the nearest ten when estimating how many dots on a ladybird or choosing to estimate to the nearest thousand when estimating crowd sizes at a venue

elaborations.name: VC2M3N06-E04 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: checking the reasonableness of an addition calculation by using two- and three-digit numbers to the nearest ten or hundred to estimate; for example, using 200 + 400 = 600 to estimate and check the solution to the calculation 219 + 385

strand_content_descriptions.name: VC2M3N07 - Mathematics
strand_content_descriptions.text: recognise the relationships between dollars and cents and represent money values in different ways

elaborations.name: VC2M3N07-E01 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: investigating the relationship between dollars and cents, using physical or virtual materials to make different combinations of the same amount of money

elaborations.name: VC2M3N07-E02 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: representing money amounts in different ways using knowledge of part-part-whole relationships; for example, knowing that $1 is equal to 100 cents, representing $1.85 as $1 + 50c + 20c + 10c + 5c or 50c + 50c + 50c + 10c + 10c + 10c + 5c; or when calculating change from buying an item for $1.30 from $2, starting from $1.30 and adding 20c and 50c, which gives $2

strand_content_descriptions.name: VC2M3N08 - Mathematics
strand_content_descriptions.text: use mathematical modelling to solve practical problems involving additive and multiplicative situations, including financial contexts; formulate problems using number sentences and choose calculation strategies, using digital tools where appropriate; interpret and communicate solutions in terms of the situation

elaborations.name: VC2M3N08-E01 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: modelling practical additive situations, choosing whether to use an addition, subtraction or both when representing the problem as a number sentence, and explaining how each number in their number sentence is connected to the situation

elaborations.name: VC2M3N08-E02 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: modelling additive problems using a bar model to represent the problem; for example, modelling the problem ‘I had 75 tomatoes and then picked some more. Now I have 138. How many did I pick?’

elaborations.name: VC2M3N08-E03 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: modelling practical multiplicative situations using materials or a diagram to represent the problem; for example, if 4 tomato plants each have 6 tomatoes, deciding whether to use an addition or multiplication number sentence, explaining how each number in their number sentence is connected to the situation

elaborations.name: VC2M3N08-E04 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: modelling and solving practical division problems involving unknown numbers of groups or finding how much is in each group by representing the problem with both division and multiplication number sentences, and explaining how the 2 number sentences are connected to the problem

elaborations.name: VC2M3N08-E05 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: modelling the problem of deciding how to share an amount equally (for example, 48 horses into 2, 4, 6 or 8 paddocks), representing the shares with a division and a multiplication number sentence, and counting the number in each share to check the solutions

strand_content_descriptions.name: VC2M3N09 - Mathematics
strand_content_descriptions.text: follow and create algorithms involving a sequence of steps and decisions to investigate numbers; describe any emerging patterns

elaborations.name: VC2M3N09-E01 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: following or creating an algorithm to generate number patterns formed by doubling and halving using technology to assist, where appropriate, and identifying and describing emerging patterns

elaborations.name: VC2M3N09-E02 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: following or creating an algorithm that determines whether a given number is a multiple of 2, 5 or 10, identifying and discussing emerging patterns

elaborations.name: VC2M3N09-E03 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: creating an algorithm as a set of instructions that a classmate can follow to generate multiples of 3 using the rule ‘To multiply by 3 you double the number and add on one more of the number’ (for example, for 3 threes, you double 3 and add on 3 to get 9; for 3 fours you double 4 and add one more 4 to get 12 …)

elaborations.name: VC2M3N09-E04 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: creating a sorting algorithm that will sort a collection of 5-cent and 10-cent coins and providing the total value of the collection by applying knowledge of multiples of 5 and 10

strand_content_descriptions.name: VC2M3A01 - Mathematics
strand_content_descriptions.text: recognise and explain the connection between addition and subtraction as inverse operations, apply to partition numbers and find unknown values in number sentences

elaborations.name: VC2M3A01-E01 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: partitioning numbers using materials, part-part-whole diagrams or bar models, and recording addition and subtraction facts for each representation, explaining how each fact is connected to the materials, diagrams or models (for example, 16 + 8 = 24, 24 − 8 = 16, 8 = 24 − 16)

elaborations.name: VC2M3A01-E02 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: using the inverse relationship between addition and subtraction to find unknown values with a calculator or by counting on; for example, representing the problem ‘Peter had some money and then spent $375. Now he has $158 left. How much did Peter have to start with?’ as □ − $375 = $158 and solving the problem using $375 + $158 = $533; or solving 27 + □ = 63 using subtraction, □ = 63 – 27, or by counting on 27, 37, 47, 57, 60, 63, so add 3 tens and 6 ones, so □ = 36

elaborations.name: VC2M3A01-E03 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: exploring Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ stories and dances that show the connection between addition and subtraction, representing this as a number sentence and discussing how this conveys important information about balance in processes on Country/Place

strand_content_descriptions.name: VC2M3A02 - Mathematics
strand_content_descriptions.text: extend and apply knowledge of addition and subtraction facts to 20 to develop efficient mental strategies for computation with larger numbers without a calculator

elaborations.name: VC2M3A02-E01 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: partitioning using materials and part-part-whole diagrams to develop subtraction facts related to addition facts, such as 8 + 7 = 15 therefore 15 − 7 = 8 and 15 − 8 = 7

elaborations.name: VC2M3A02-E02 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: using partitioning to develop and record facts systematically (for example, ‘How many ways can 12 monkeys be spread among 2 trees?’, 12 = 12 + 0, 12 = 11 + 1, 12 = 10 + 2, 12 = 9 + 3, …), explaining how they know they have found all possible partitions

elaborations.name: VC2M3A02-E03 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: understanding basic addition and related subtraction facts and using extensions to these facts; for example, 6 + 6 = 12, 16 + 6 = 22, 6 + 7 = 13, 16 + 7 = 23, and 60 + 60 = 120, 600 + 600 = 1200

strand_content_descriptions.name: VC2M3A03 - Mathematics
strand_content_descriptions.text: recall and demonstrate proficiency with multiplication facts for 3, 4, 5 and 10; extend and apply facts to develop the related division facts

elaborations.name: VC2M3A03-E01 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: using concrete or virtual materials, groups and repeated addition to recognise patterns and establish the 3, 4, 5 and 10 multiplication facts; for example, using the language of ‘3 groups of 2 equals 6’ to develop into ‘3 twos are 6’ and extend to establish the 3 × 10 multiplication facts and related division facts

elaborations.name: VC2M3A03-E02 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: recognising that when they multiply a number by 5, the resulting number will either end in a 5 or a zero; and using a calculator or spreadsheet to generate a list of the multiples of 5 to develop the multiplication and related division facts for fives

elaborations.name: VC2M3A03-E03 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: practising calculating and deriving multiplication facts for 3, 4, 5 and 10, explaining and recalling the patterns in them and using them to derive related division facts

elaborations.name: VC2M3A03-E04 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: systematically exploring algorithms used for repeated addition, comparing and describing what is happening, and using them to establish the multiplication facts for 3, 4, 5 and 10; for example, following the sequence of steps, the decisions being made and the resulting solution, recognising and generalising any emerging patterns

strand_content_descriptions.name: VC2M3M01 - Mathematics
strand_content_descriptions.text: identify which metric units are used to measure everyday items; use measurements of familiar items and known units to make estimates

elaborations.name: VC2M3M01-E01 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: examining the packaging on supermarket items to determine the metric unit used to describe the mass or volume of the contents

elaborations.name: VC2M3M01-E02 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: identifying items that have a mass of one kilogram or 500 grams, or a capacity of one litre or 500 millilitres, and using these benchmarks to estimate the mass or capacity of other things, explaining their reasoning

elaborations.name: VC2M3M01-E03 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: estimating the height of a tree by comparing it to the height of their friend and quoting the result as ‘The tree is about 3 times as tall’; and estimating the capacity of a fish tank by using a litre milk carton as a benchmark

elaborations.name: VC2M3M01-E04 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: choosing and using metres to estimate the dimensions of the classroom

strand_content_descriptions.name: VC2M3M02 - Mathematics
strand_content_descriptions.text: measure and compare objects using familiar metric units of length, mass and capacity, and instruments with labelled markings

elaborations.name: VC2M3M02-E01 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: making a measuring tape using metric units of length and using it to measure and compare things, for example, the girth of a tree; and explaining that the lines on a ruler show the beginning and end of each unit

elaborations.name: VC2M3M02-E02 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: using a strip of one-centimetre grid paper to measure and compare the length of objects, connecting this with centimetre units on a ruler and using fractions of a graduation to give a more accurate measure

elaborations.name: VC2M3M02-E03 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: discussing how the capacity of a container or object usually refers to the amount of liquid it can hold, measured in millilitres and litres, and comparing the capacity of different sizes of familiar drinks (for example, 600-millilitre, one-litre, 2-litre and 3-litre milk containers)

elaborations.name: VC2M3M02-E04 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: measuring and comparing the mass of objects and capacity of containers, using measuring jugs and kitchen or other scales and standard metric units of millilitres, litres, grams and kilograms; and interpreting and explaining what the lines on the measuring jug or scales mean

elaborations.name: VC2M3M02-E05 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: comparing the capacity of different beakers used in science lessons and using the numbered graduations to measure out different capacities of liquid

strand_content_descriptions.name: VC2M3M03 - Mathematics
strand_content_descriptions.text: recognise and use the relationship between formal units of time, including days, hours, minutes and seconds, to estimate and compare the duration of events

elaborations.name: VC2M3M03-E01 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: estimating how long it would take to read a set passage of text, and sharing this information to demonstrate understanding of formal units of duration of time

elaborations.name: VC2M3M03-E02 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: planning a sequence of events based on estimates of the duration of each event; for example, planning a set of activities for a class party by estimating how long each game or activity will take

elaborations.name: VC2M3M03-E03 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: reading or setting the time on digital devices to the minute or second; for example, setting an online timing device to count down from a set time, or setting the time on a digital clock

elaborations.name: VC2M3M03-E04 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: using sand timers and digital timers to measure and check estimates of short durations of time, such as one minute, 3 minutes and 5 minutes

elaborations.name: VC2M3M03-E05 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: exploring how cultural accounts of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples explain cycles of time that involve the sun, moon and stars

strand_content_descriptions.name: VC2M3M04 - Mathematics
strand_content_descriptions.text: describe the relationship between the hours and minutes on analog and digital clocks, and read the time to the nearest minute

elaborations.name: VC2M3M04-E01 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: representing and reading the time on an analog clock using the markings and the positions of the hands, to the nearest minute mark or 5-minute interval

elaborations.name: VC2M3M04-E02 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: reading and connecting analog and digital time, interpreting times, and recognising and using the language of time, for example, 12:15 as a quarter past 12, or 15 minutes past 12; 12:45 as a quarter to one or 15 minutes before one o’clock; and 10:05 as 5 minutes past 10

elaborations.name: VC2M3M04-E03 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: reading analog clocks throughout the day, and noticing and connecting the position of the hour hand and the distance the minute hand has travelled during the current hour

strand_content_descriptions.name: VC2M3M05 - Mathematics
strand_content_descriptions.text: identify angles as measures of turn and use right angles as a reference to compare angles in everyday situations

elaborations.name: VC2M3M05-E01 - Mathematics

elaborations.name: VC2M3P01-E03 - Mathematics

strand_content_descriptions.name: VC2M3P02 - Mathematics

elaborations.name: VC2M3P02-E01 - Mathematics

elaborations.name: VC2M3P02-E02 - Mathematics

curriculum_level_description.body:
In Level 4, learning in Mathematics builds on each student’s prior learning and experiences. Students engage in a range of approaches to the learning and doing of mathematics that develop their understanding of and fluency with concepts, procedures and processes by making connections, reasoning, problem-solving and practice. Proficiency in mathematics enables students to respond to familiar and unfamiliar situations by employing mathematical strategies to make informed decisions and solve problems efficiently.

Students further develop proficiency and positive dispositions towards mathematics and its use as they:

  • consolidate their knowledge and facility with arithmetic operations, and draw on their proficiency with number facts, fractions and decimals, to deepen their appreciation of how numbers work
  • develop and use strategies for multiplication that are based on their understanding of multiplication as an operation and their knowledge of laws for arithmetic operations
  • choose and use efficient mental and written strategies when modelling problems, communicating their solutions within the context of the situation
  • use algorithms to generate sets of numbers, recognising and describing any patterns that emerge
  • become aware of the importance of context and purpose when they make judgements and reflect on the reasonableness of measurements and the results of calculations, and how they choose to represent mathematics and mathematical information
  • measure and estimate common attributes of objects using conventional instruments and appropriate metric units
  • develop and use surveys to obtain data that is directly relevant to their statistical investigations
  • draw on their reasoning skills to analyse, categorise and order chance events and identify independent and dependent events
  • investigate variability by conducting repeated chance experiments and observing results.

curriculum_achievement_standard.body:
By the end of Level 4, students use their understanding of place value to represent tenths and hundredths in decimal form and to multiply natural numbers by multiples of 10. Students use mathematical modelling to solve financial and other practical problems, formulating the problem using number sentences, solving the problem choosing efficient strategies and interpreting the results in terms of the situation. They use their proficiency with addition, subtraction, multiplication facts for tens (× 10) and related division facts to perform arithmetic operations to add and subtract, and multiply and divide numbers efficiently. They choose rounding and estimation strategies to determine whether results of calculations are reasonable. They recognise common equivalent fractions in familiar contexts and make connections between fraction and decimal notations. Students count and represent familiar fractions on a number line.

Students find unknown values in numerical equations involving addition and subtraction. They follow and create algorithms that generate sets of numbers and identify emerging patterns.

Students use appropriate scaled instruments and appropriate units to measure length, mass, capacity and temperature. They measure and approximate perimeters and areas for regular and irregular shapes. They convert between units of time when solving problems involving duration. Students compare angles relative to a right angle using angle names.

Students represent and approximate shapes and objects from their environment. Students create and interpret grid references. They identify line and rotational symmetry in plane shapes and create symmetrical patterns.

Students create many-to-one data displays, assess the suitability of displays for representing data and informally discuss the shape of distributions and variation in data. They use surveys and digital tools to generate categorical or discrete numerical data in statistical investigations and communicate their findings in context.

Students order events or the outcomes of chance experiments in terms of likelihood and identify whether events are independent or dependent. They conduct repeated chance experiments and describe the variation in results.

as_extracts.name: MAT4-E01
as_extracts.description: students use their understanding of place value to represent tenths and hundredths in decimal form and to multiply natural numbers by multiples of 10.

content_descriptions.name: VC2M4N01 - Mathematics
content_descriptions.text: recognise and extend the application of place value to tenths and hundredths and use the conventions of decimal notation to name and represent decimals

elaborations.name: VC2M4N01-E01 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: using a bar to represent the whole, dividing it into 10 equal pieces with each piece representing 0.1 or one-tenth of the whole length and understanding that 2 pieces are 0.2 or two-tenths of the whole

elaborations.name: VC2M4N01-E02 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: using materials to show the multiplicative relationship between the whole, tenths and hundredths; for example, using a bundle of 10 straws to represent the whole, one straw as the tenth, and cutting the tenth into 10 parts to show the hundredths; or using deci-pipes to represent tenths

elaborations.name: VC2M4N01-E03 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: recognising that one is the same as ten-tenths and one-tenth is the same as ten-hundredths and using this relationship to rename decimals; for example, renaming 0.25 as two-tenths and five-hundredths or twenty-five-hundredths

elaborations.name: VC2M4N01-E04 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: making models of measurement attributes to show the relationship between the base unit and parts of the unit, for example, 1.5 metres is one metre and five-tenths of the next metre; 1.75 units is one unit and seventy-five-hundredths of the next unit

elaborations.name: VC2M4N01-E05 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: counting large quantities of mixed notes and coins, writing the total using dollars and cents, and recognising the cents as parts of the next dollar

elaborations.name: VC2M4N01-E06 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: comparing the way money and measures are read and said, and explaining how they are the same and different; for example, explaining that $2.75 is said ‘two dollars seventy-five’ and 2.75 metres is said ‘two point seven five metres’, and recognising that the 7 means seven-tenths and the 5 means five-hundredths in both

content_descriptions.name: VC2M4N05 - Mathematics
content_descriptions.text: solve problems involving multiplying or dividing natural numbers by multiples and powers of 10 without a calculator, using the multiplicative relationship between the place value of digits

elaborations.name: VC2M4N05-E01 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: using physical or virtual materials to demonstrate the multiplicative relationship between the places

elaborations.name: VC2M4N05-E02 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: using materials such as place value charts, numeral expanders or sliders to recognise and explain why multiplying by 10 moves the digits one place to the left and dividing by 10 moves digits one place to the right

elaborations.name: VC2M4N05-E03 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: using a calculator or other digital tools to recognise and develop an understanding of the effect of multiplying or dividing numbers by tens, hundreds and thousands, recording sequences in a place value chart, in a table or spreadsheet, generalising the patterns noticed and applying them to solve multiplicative problems without a calculator

content_descriptions.name: VC2M4N09 - Mathematics
content_descriptions.text: use mathematical modelling to solve practical problems that involve additive and multiplicative situations, including financial contexts; formulate the problems using number sentences and choose efficient calculation strategies, using digital tools where appropriate; interpret and communicate solutions in terms of the situation

elaborations.name: VC2M4N09-E01 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: modelling and solving a range of practical additive problems using materials, part-part-whole diagrams and/or a bar model, and writing addition and/or subtraction number sentences, based on whether a part or the whole is missing; and explaining how each number in their number sentence is connected to the situation

elaborations.elaboration_text: modelling and solving multiplication problems involving money, such as buying 5 toy scooters for $96 each, using efficient mental strategies and written jottings to keep track if needed; for example, rounding $96 up to $100 and subtracting 5 × $4 = $20, so 5 × $96 is the same as 5 × $100 less $20, giving the answer $500 − $20 = $480

elaborations.name: VC2M4N09-E05 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: modelling situations by formulating comparison problems using number sentences, comparison models and arrays; for example, ‘Ariana read 16 books for the “readathon”; Maryam read 4 times as many books. How many books did Maryam read?’ using the expression 4 × 16 and using place value partitioning, basic facts and an array, thinking 4 × 10 = 40 and 4 × 6 = 24, so 4 × 16 can be written as 40 + 24 = 64

as_extracts.description: They use their proficiency with addition, subtraction, multiplication facts for tens (× 10) and related division facts to perform arithmetic operations to add and subtract, and multiply and divide numbers efficiently.

elaborations.name: VC2M4N06-E01 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: using and choosing efficient calculation strategies for addition and subtraction problems involving larger numbers, for example, place value partitioning, inverse relationship, compatible numbers, jump strategies, bridging tens, splitting one or more numbers, extensions to basic facts, algorithms and digital tools where appropriate

elaborations.name: VC2M4N06-E02 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: using physical or virtual materials to demonstrate doubling and halving strategies for solving multiplication problems; for example, for 5 × 18, using the fact that double 5 is 10 and half of 18 is 9; or using 10 × 18 = 180, then halving 180 to get 90; or applying the associative property of multiplication, where 5 × 18 becomes 5 × 2 × 9, then 5 × 2 × 9 = 10 × 9 = 90 so that 5 × 18 = 90

elaborations.name: VC2M4N06-E03 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: using an array to represent a multiplication problem, connecting the idea of how many groups and how many in each group with the rows and columns of the array, and writing an associated number sentence

elaborations.name: VC2M4N06-E04 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: using materials or a diagram to solve a multiplication or division problem, by writing a number sentence and explaining what each of the numbers within the number sentence refers to

elaborations.name: VC2M4N06-E05 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: representing a multiplicative situation using materials, array diagrams and/or a bar model, and writing multiplication and/or division number sentences, based on whether the number of groups, the number per group or the total is missing, and explaining how each number in their number sentence is connected to the situation

elaborations.name: VC2M4N06-E06 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: using place value partitioning, basic facts and an area or region model to represent and solve multiplication problems; for example, for 16 × 4, thinking 10 × 4 and 6 × 4, then 40 + 24 = 64, or a double double strategy where double 16 is 32, double this is 64, so 16 × 4 is 64

content_descriptions.name: VC2M4A02 - Mathematics
content_descriptions.text: recall and demonstrate proficiency with multiplication facts up to 10 × 10 and related division facts, and explain the patterns in these; extend and apply facts to develop efficient mental and written strategies for computation with larger numbers without a calculator

elaborations.name: VC2M4A02-E01 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: using arrays on grid paper or created with blocks or counters to develop, represent and explain patterns in multiplication facts up to 10 × 10; and using the arrays to explain the related division facts

elaborations.name: VC2M4A02-E02 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: using materials or diagrams to develop and record multiplication strategies such as doubling, halving, commutativity and adding one more or subtracting from a group to reach a known fact; for example, creating multiples of 3 on grid paper and doubling to find multiples of 6, and recording and explaining the connections to the × 3 and × 6 multiplication facts: 3, 6, 9, … doubled is 6, 12, 18, …

elaborations.name: VC2M4A02-E03 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: using known multiplication facts for 2, 3, 5 and 10 to establish multiplication facts for 4, 6, 7, 8 and 9 in different ways; for example, using multiples of 10 to establish the multiples of 9 as ‘to multiply a number by 9 you multiply by 10 then take the number away’: 9 × 4 = 10 × 4 − 4, so 9 × 4 is 40 − 4 = 36; or using multiples of 3 as ‘to multiply a number by 9 you multiply by 3, and then multiply the result by 3 again’

elaborations.name: VC2M4A02-E04 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: using arrays and known multiplication facts for twos and fives to develop the multiplication facts for sevens, applying the distributive property of multiplication; for example, when finding 6 × 7, knowing that 7 is made up of 2 and 5, and using an array to show that 6 × 7 is the same as 6 × 2 + 6 × 5 = 12 + 30, which is 42

as_extracts.name: MAT4-E04
as_extracts.description: They choose rounding and estimation strategies to determine whether results of calculations are reasonable.

content_descriptions.name: VC2M4N07 - Mathematics
content_descriptions.text: choose and use estimation and rounding to check and explain the reasonableness of calculations, including the results of financial transactions

elaborations.name: VC2M4N07-E01 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: using proficiency with basic facts to estimate the result of a calculation and say what amounts the answer will be between; for example, 5 packets of biscuits at $2.60 each will cost between $10 and $15 as 5 × $2 = $10 and 5 × $3 = $15

elaborations.name: VC2M4N07-E02 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: using rounded amounts to complete an estimated budget for a shopping trip or an excursion, explaining why overestimating the amounts is appropriate

elaborations.name: VC2M4N07-E03 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: recognising the effect of rounding in addition and multiplication calculations; rounding both numbers up, both numbers down, and one number up and one number down, and explaining which is the best approximation and why

as_extracts.name: MAT4-E05
as_extracts.description: They recognise common equivalent fractions in familiar contexts and make connections between fraction and decimal notations.

content_descriptions.name: VC2M4N03 - Mathematics
content_descriptions.text: find equivalent representations of fractions using related denominators and make connections between fractions and decimal notation

elaborations.name: VC2M4N03-E01 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: extending fraction families within collections of materials, for example, by seeing $\frac{3}{4}$ as 3 in each 4, showing this within related fractions like $\frac{6}{8}$ or seeing that $\frac{2}{5}$ means 2 in each 5 so it can be shown within $\frac{4}{10}$

elaborations.name: VC2M4N03-E02 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: creating models of equivalent fractions by subdividing capacity measures into smaller fractions; for example, half a cup of flour could be shown as two-quarters or four-eighths of a cup of flour

elaborations.name: VC2M4N03-E03 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: folding paper to show equivalence between different fractions; for example, folding A4 paper in half and half again, repeating to form eighths and demonstrating that $\frac{4}{8}=\frac{2}{4}=\frac{1}{2}$; or folding paper strips into fifths and tenths, and recording as both fractions and decimals

elaborations.name: VC2M4N03-E04 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: identifying and using the connection between fractions of metres and decimals; for example, finding $\frac{1}{4}$ of a metre and connecting this to 0.25 metres or 25 centimetres, or finding $\frac{1}{10}$ of a metre and connecting this with 0.10 metres or 10 centimetres

elaborations.name: VC2M4N03-E05 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: using array diagrams to show the relationship between fractions and division and multiplication of natural numbers, for example, 3 × 4 = 12, 12 ÷ 4 = 3, $\frac{1}{4}$ of 12 is 3, $\frac{1}{3}$ of 12 is 4

as_extracts.name: MAT4-E06
as_extracts.description: Students count and represent familiar fractions on a number line.

content_descriptions.name: VC2M4N04 - Mathematics
content_descriptions.text: count by multiples of quarters, halves and thirds, including mixed numerals; locate and represent these fractions as numbers on number lines

elaborations.name: VC2M4N04-E01 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: cutting objects such as oranges or sandwiches into quarters and counting by quarters to find the total number, and saying the counting sequence ‘one-quarter, two-quarters, three-quarters, four-quarters or one-whole, five-quarters or one-and-one-quarter, six-quarters or one-and-two-quarters … eight-quarters or two-wholes ...’

elaborations.name: VC2M4N04-E02 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: subdividing the sections between whole numbers on parallel number lines so that one shows halves, another shows quarters and one other shows thirds; and counting the fractions by jumping along the number lines, and noticing when the count is at the same position on the parallel lines

elaborations.name: VC2M4N04-E03 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: converting mixed numerals into improper fractions and vice versa, and representing mixed numerals on a number line

elaborations.name: VC2M4N04-E04 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: using a number line to represent and count in tenths, recognising that 10 tenths is equivalent to one

as_extracts.name: MAT4-E07
as_extracts.description: Students find unknown values in numerical equations involving addition and subtraction.

content_descriptions.name: VC2M4A01 - Mathematics
content_descriptions.text: find unknown values in numerical equations involving addition and subtraction, using the properties of numbers and operations

elaborations.name: VC2M4A01-E01 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: demonstrating the commutative properties of addition using materials, diagrams and number lines; for example, using number lines to demonstrate that 5 + 2 = 2 + 5, and demonstrating that 2 + 2 + 3 = 7 and 2 + 3 + 2 = 7 and 3 + 2 + 2 = 7

elaborations.name: VC2M4A01-E02 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: using balance scales and informal uniform units to create addition or subtraction number sentences showing equivalence, such as 7 + 8 = 6 + 9, and to find unknowns in equivalent number sentences, such as 6 + 8 = □ + 10

elaborations.name: VC2M4A01-E03 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: using relational thinking and knowledge of equivalent number sentences to explain whether equations involving addition or subtraction are true; for example, explaining that 27 − 14 = 17 − 4 is true and using a number line to show the common difference is 13

as_extracts.name: MAT4-E08
as_extracts.description: They follow and create algorithms that generate sets of numbers and identify emerging patterns.

content_descriptions.name: VC2M4N10 - Mathematics
content_descriptions.text: follow and create algorithms involving a sequence of steps and decisions that use addition or multiplication to generate sets of numbers; identify and describe any emerging patterns

elaborations.name: VC2M4N10-E01 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: creating an algorithm that will generate number sequences involving multiples of one to 10 using digital tools to assist, identifying and explaining emerging patterns, and recognising that number sequences can be extended indefinitely

elaborations.name: VC2M4N10-E02 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: creating a basic flow chart that represents an algorithm that will generate a sequence of numbers using multiplication by a constant term; using a calculator to model and follow the algorithm, and recording the sequence of numbers generated; and checking results and describing any emerging patterns

elaborations.name: VC2M4N10-E03 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: using a multiplication formula in a spreadsheet and the ‘fill down’ function to generate a sequence of numbers (for example, entering the number ‘1’ in the cell A1, using ‘fill down’ to cell A100, entering the formula ‘=A1*4’ in the cell B1 and using the ‘fill down’ function to generate a sequence of 100 numbers) and describing emerging patterns

elaborations.name: VC2M4N10-E04 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: creating an algorithm that will generate number sequences involving multiples of one to 10, using digital tools to assist, identifying and explaining emerging patterns, and recognising that number sequences can be extended indefinitely

as_extracts.name: MAT4-E09
as_extracts.description: Students use appropriate scaled instruments and appropriate units to measure length, mass, capacity and temperature.

content_descriptions.name: VC2M4M01 - Mathematics
content_descriptions.text: use scaled and digital instruments to interpret unmarked and partial units to measure and compare lengths, masses, capacities, durations and temperatures, using appropriate units

elaborations.name: VC2M4M01-E01 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: reading the mass of objects measured with digital and analog kitchen scales and explaining what unit of mass the lines on the analog scales refer to

elaborations.name: VC2M4M01-E02 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: deciding on which attribute, unit and measuring instrument to use to compare the length and mass of various things, such as the distance travelled by an object in a science investigation; and explaining the use of units such as grams or millimetres to give accurate measures when needed

elaborations.name: VC2M4M01-E03 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: using scaled instruments such as tape measures, measuring jugs, kitchen scales and thermometers to record measures using whole units (for example, 560 millimetres) or whole and part units (for example, 5.25 metres, 1.75 litres, 2.5 kilograms, 28.5° Celsius)

elaborations.name: VC2M4M01-E04 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: reading and interpreting the scale of an analog clock without marked minutes to estimate the time to the nearest minute and to determine the duration of time between events

elaborations.name: VC2M4M01-E05 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: using the timer or alarm function of a clock to alert when a specified duration has elapsed from a given starting time, for example, for the different activities of an exercise routine

elaborations.name: VC2M4M01-E06 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: making a scaled measuring instrument such as a tape measure, ruler, sand timer, sundial or measuring cup using scaled instruments and direct comparisons

elaborations.name: VC2M4M01-E07 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: exploring the different types of scaled instruments used by Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander ranger groups and other groups to make decisions about caring for Country/Place, and modelling these in local contexts

as_extracts.name: MAT4-E10
as_extracts.description: They measure and approximate perimeters and areas for regular and irregular shapes.

content_descriptions.name: VC2M4M02 - Mathematics
content_descriptions.text: recognise ways of measuring and approximating the perimeter and area of shapes and enclosed spaces, using appropriate formal and informal units

elaborations.name: VC2M4M02-E01 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: recognising that perimeter is the sum of the lengths that form the boundary of a shape or enclosed space; choosing suitable units from a range of objects to measure around the boundary of a shape such as a garden bed; comparing the results to say which unit was an appropriate choice for the context; and using a piece of string or rope to measure the perimeter of irregular shapes and enclosed spaces, including those that have curved sections

elaborations.name: VC2M4M02-E02 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: creating a range of rectangles representing ‘paddocks’ on grid paper and establishing different methods of working out the length of the boundary fences; and explaining that the more efficient methods involve adding the side lengths rather than counting squares

elaborations.name: VC2M4M02-E03 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: recognising that area is the space enclosed by the boundary of a shape or the surface of an object; measuring and comparing the area of shapes using an array of paper tiles or mosaic squares, including part units to fill gaps at the edge of the shapes; and comparing the total areas by combining the fractional parts to make whole units

elaborations.name: VC2M4M02-E04 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: demonstrating how to use one unit repeatedly to measure the area of a shape (for example, using one paper square to measure and compare the area of a rectangle and a triangle) and recording and explaining how they used part units to give a more accurate measure, and why they needed to ensure there were no gaps or overlaps

elaborations.name: VC2M4M02-E05 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: investigating the ways Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander ranger groups and other groups measure areas of land to make decisions about fire burns to care for Country/Place

as_extracts.name: MAT4-E11
as_extracts.description: They convert between units of time when solving problems involving duration.

content_descriptions.name: VC2M4M03 - Mathematics
content_descriptions.text: solve problems involving the duration of time including situations involving ‘am’ and ‘pm’ and conversions between units of time

elaborations.name: VC2M4M03-E01 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: calculating the amount of time between 2 events, such as the start and finish of a movie, a bus journey or a flight, including cases where the starting and finishing times are written using ‘am’ and ‘pm’ notation

elaborations.name: VC2M4M03-E02 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: converting units of time using relationships between units, such as 60 minutes in an hour and 60 seconds in a minute, to solve problems; for example, creating a daily timetable for an activity such as an athletics carnival or planning an exercise routine with activities and rests

elaborations.name: VC2M4M03-E03 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: exploring Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ explanations of the passing of time through cultural accounts about cyclic phenomena involving the sun, moon and stars

as_extracts.name: MAT4-E12
as_extracts.description: Students compare angles relative to a right angle using angle names.

content_descriptions.name: VC2M4M04 - Mathematics
content_descriptions.text: estimate and compare angles using angle names including acute, obtuse, straight angle, reflex and revolution, and recognise their relationship to a right angle

elaborations.name: VC2M4M04-E01 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: classifying the interior angles of a range of shapes, using examples of angles to identify acute, obtuse, right and reflex angles

elaborations.name: VC2M4M04-E02 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: identifying angles within the environment and estimating whether they are acute, obtuse, right or reflex

elaborations.name: VC2M4M04-E03 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: creating a right-angle template using cardboard or a double-folded piece of paper and using it to compare angles in the environment, commenting on whether they are smaller than or greater than a right angle

elaborations.name: VC2M4M04-E04 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: using different measuring tools such as a spirit level or set squares to determine whether lines or objects are straight, square or perpendicular (at right angles)

as_extracts.name: MAT4-E13
as_extracts.description: Students represent and approximate shapes and objects from their environment.

content_descriptions.name: VC2M4SP01 - Mathematics
content_descriptions.text: explain and compare the geometric properties of two-dimensional shapes and three-dimensional objects

elaborations.name: VC2M4SP01-E01 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: describing the similarities and differences between two-dimensional shapes and three-dimensional objects

elaborations.name: VC2M4SP01-E02 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: recognising two-dimensional shapes that are the faces for three-dimensional objects such as prisms, pyramids and platonic solids (including tetrahedrons, cubes and dodecahedrons)

content_descriptions.name: VC2M4SP02 - Mathematics
content_descriptions.text: represent and approximate composite shapes and objects in the environment, using combinations of familiar shapes and objects

elaborations.name: VC2M4SP02-E01 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: identifying common shapes that form part of a composite shape by re-creating these shapes using physical or virtual materials

elaborations.name: VC2M4SP02-E02 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: physically or virtually using cubes to make three-dimensional models that approximate real objects; for example, building a virtual environment by using a computer software program to construct objects out of cubes

elaborations.name: VC2M4SP02-E03 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: approximating complex shapes and objects in the environment with familiar shapes and objects; for example, drawing cartoon animals by combining familiar shapes

elaborations.name: VC2M4SP02-E04 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: recognising how familiar shapes and objects are used in logos and other graphics to represent more complex shapes, and creating logos using graphic design software

as_extracts.name: MAT4-E14
as_extracts.description: Students create and interpret grid references.

content_descriptions.name: VC2M4SP03 - Mathematics
content_descriptions.text: create and interpret grid reference systems using grid references and directions to locate and describe positions and pathways

elaborations.name: VC2M4SP03-E01 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: interpreting a grid reference map of a familiar location of interest, such as a map of the showgrounds, a food festival, botanical garden, a park in the local area or a train station, and writing instructions using grid references for a friend to find them at a specified location

elaborations.name: VC2M4SP03-E02 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: recognising that a spreadsheet uses a grid reference system, locating and entering data in cells, and using a spreadsheet to record data collected through observations or experiments

elaborations.name: VC2M4SP03-E03 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: comparing and contrasting, describing and locating landmarks, people or things in a bird’s-eye picture of a busy scene, such as people in a park, initially without a transparent grid reference system overlaid on the picture and then with the grid overlaid; and noticing how the grid helps to pinpoint things quickly and easily

elaborations.name: VC2M4SP03-E04 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: using different-sized grids as a tool to enlarge an image or artwork

as_extracts.name: MAT4-E15
as_extracts.description: They identify line and rotational symmetry in plane shapes and create symmetrical patterns.

content_descriptions.name: VC2M4SP04 - Mathematics
content_descriptions.text: recognise line and rotational symmetry of shapes and create symmetrical patterns and pictures, using dynamic geometry software where appropriate

elaborations.name: VC2M4SP04-E01 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: identifying rotational symmetry of shapes by tracing around various shapes and objects to create an image, and using the image to test and record which different rotations result in the same image

elaborations.name: VC2M4SP04-E02 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: using dynamic geometry software to manipulate shapes and create symmetrical patterns; for example, creating tessellation patterns that are symmetrical

elaborations.name: VC2M4SP04-E03 - Mathematics
elaborations.elaboration_text: using stimulus materials such as the motifs in Central Asian textiles, Tibetan artefacts, Indian lotus designs and Islamic artwork to investigate and discuss line and rotational symmetry
